evidence_base.sufficiency_note: 16 sessions across 9 months and 5 subjects, with a clean split between self-directed and assigned work, supports a genuine profile.

cognitive_types.label: Fluency
cognitive_types.definition: Retrieving or recalling known material fast and automatically
cognitive_types.summary: No dedicated recall-and-confirm turns appear. Her sessions are either advanced material she's building from scratch or homework she's declined to engage with at all — neither produces the quick, settled-fact retrieval this type looks like.

cognitive_types.label: Procedural
cognitive_types.definition: Executing a known sequence correctly, step by step
cognitive_types.summary: Split cleanly in two: procedural work she's already mastered gets handed off wholesale (logs, rational functions), while procedural work embedded in something she chose herself — redoing a measurability proof correctly — gets driven end to end.

snippets.subject: Mathematics
snippets.unit: Self-directed — uncle's measure theory problem set

preceding_ai_turn.text: The measure computation and the final answer of 0 are correct, but there's a gap: you asserted A is measurable because it 'looks sparse,' without showing it. 'Looks nice' isn't a measurability argument on its own — you need to actually construct A as something you know is measurable, like a countable intersection of measurable sets.

student_turn.text: ok let me redo it properly: A = intersection over n of A_n, where A_n is numbers with a non-7 digit in position n. each A_n is a finite union of closed intervals so it's measurable, and measurable sets are closed under countable intersection, so A is measurable. then the measure computation I already had holds and gives 0.

snippets.why: She rebuilds the full argument correctly from the corrected principle, unprompted, in her own words.

cognitive_types.label: Conceptual
cognitive_types.definition: Building or repairing a mental model of how something works
cognitive_types.summary: Her single strongest and most consistent category. In session after session she states her own working model, tests it against a worry she generated herself, and revises it live in the transcript — not just once, as a peak, but as the default mode of her self-directed sessions.

snippets.subject: Science

preceding_ai_turn.text: In rigorous treatments, convergence is checked — often via bounding the terms or invoking a theorem specific to the expansion. In practice, especially in perturbation theory, physicists often work formally without proving absolute convergence, because the series may not even converge at all in the usual sense — many perturbation series are asymptotic, not convergent. The safety comes from decades of the results matching experiment, not from a term-by-term convergence proof every time.

student_turn.text: wait so it's not actually that physics is automatically safe from the rearrangement problem, it's that either the series happens to converge absolutely, or it doesn't even converge in the first place and they're doing something else entirely that isn't covered by the theorem either way. that's a different claim than 'physics doesn't have this problem'

snippets.why: She corrects her own opening premise on logical grounds and states the sharper, more precise version herself.

snippets.subject: Computer Science

preceding_ai_turn.text: It doesn't use timestamps — generational collectors allocate new objects into a separate memory region (often called a nursery). Age is implicit in which region the object lives in; objects that survive a collection get promoted to an older region.

student_turn.text: oh, so the region IS the timestamp, you don't need to store one anywhere because location already encodes age. that's actually elegant, I was assuming it had to be metadata attached to the object itself

snippets.why: The clearest single moment of a wrong assumption being named and repaired live, in one sentence, in her own words.

cognitive_types.label: Critical Thinking
cognitive_types.definition: Evaluating, reasoning about, or challenging a claim
cognitive_types.summary: Skeptical of consensus claims, not just of the tutor — she repeatedly declines to accept 'most people believe X' or 'this is the standard answer' without asking what's actually holding the claim up.

snippets.subject: Computer Science

preceding_ai_turn.text: Open. Formally: P is the class of problems solvable in polynomial time; NP is the class where a proposed solution can be *verified* in polynomial time. Whether P=NP is unproven either way, though the general belief among researchers is P≠NP, based on decades of failed attempts to find polynomial algorithms for NP-complete problems.

student_turn.text: ok but 'most people believe' isn't an argument, it's a headcount. what's the actual reasoning behind leaning P≠NP if nobody's proved it

snippets.why: She rejects an appeal to consensus outright and demands the actual structural justification.

snippets.subject: Mathematics
snippets.unit: Self-directed — Gödel's incompleteness theorem (beyond Algebra II)

preceding_ai_turn.text: Roughly: in any formal system powerful enough to express basic arithmetic, if the system is consistent, there will be true statements about numbers that the system cannot prove. Gödel did this by encoding statements about the system as numbers, so the system could effectively make a statement about itself — something like 'this statement cannot be proved within this system.'

student_turn.text: wait, that's the same trick Cantor used isn't it. encoding things as numbers so you can build a statement that refers to the whole list it's supposed to be part of, like the diagonal argument for uncountability. is that actually the same move or am I forcing a connection that isn't there

snippets.why: She independently proposes a structural connection between two different fields and checks it rather than assuming it.

snippets.subject: Mathematics
snippets.unit: Self-directed — Gödel's incompleteness theorem (beyond Algebra II)

preceding_ai_turn.text: For almost all working mathematics, it's an asterisk. The unprovable statements Gödel's construction produces are weird self-referential ones, not the kind of statement you run into proving, say, a theorem about groups. Where it does bite in practice: things like the continuum hypothesis, shown independent of standard set theory — not provable or disprovable from the usual axioms. That's a real, non-contrived example.

student_turn.text: ok that's kind of unsettling actually, in a good way. I'm going to go find the actual paper instead of just explanations of it

snippets.why: She sets her own next step beyond the conversation rather than just closing it out.

teacher_actions.action: Require one sentence of her own reaction or thesis before she can ask for a full draft on a writing assignment — the same nudge the tutor already tries and she currently overrides.
teacher_actions.rationale: Every writing-shaped assignment (two English tasks, the History essay) was a clean offload; every self-directed session opened with her own reasoning first. The split is task-shaped, not ability-shaped.

teacher_actions.action: Swap routine worksheets on content she's already scored 90%+ on (logs, rational functions) for a problem that costs her something — an extension or a 'find where this method breaks' prompt.
teacher_actions.rationale: Her clean procedural offloads were exclusively on material with nothing left in it for her to learn, not evidence of avoiding difficulty in general.

teacher_actions.action: Give her a standing, ungraded weekly prompt to connect current class material to whatever she's chasing on her own time.
teacher_actions.rationale: Transfer appeared four times, unprompted, at real depth — unusually frequent for this type — including one instance where she explicitly linked two of her own earlier sessions into a single self-assessment. This is a proven, habitual capability with no classroom outlet.

teacher_actions.action: Ask her directly, once a grading period, what she actually got out of an assignment versus what grade it earned.
teacher_actions.rationale: Turn 93 is the clearest statement in the transcript of the gap driving her whole profile — she can name her own motivation precisely the moment she's asked, and almost nothing in her graded work currently asks.

caveats: This reflects one AI tutor across one school year; it doesn't see in-class work, the uncle's own problem sets outside any recorded system, or conversations with teachers.
Sessions are self-selected — she brought what she was stuck on or curious about, which skews away from routine work she handles without asking for help at all.
Depth ratings reflect what she wrote in the moment, not independently verified retention.
The split between self-directed and assigned-homework sessions may partly reflect which kind of task she chooses to bring to an AI tutor at all, not only how she engages once there.
